newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP says SPD doesn't want deal on taxes.
newsitem.headline: German FDP says SPD doesn't want deal on taxes.

text.p: Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), junior partner in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition, said on Wednesday the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) had no interest in reaching a compromise deal on tax reforms.
FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms accused SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine of leading a "pre-Easter tax dance".

Solms said Kohl's three-party coalition would go ahead and submit legislation to parliament which would pave the way for implementing a 30 billion mark package of corporate and income tax cuts it agreed on in January.

The Kohl cabinet on Tuesday approved Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1998 tax bill, which would cut corporate and commercial tax rates and unify them at 40 percent in a move offset by tightening up on writeoff opportunities.
The bill would also cut the solidarity income tax surcharge by two points to 5.5 percent, lightening the tax burden by 7.5 billion marks.
Despite coalition plans to legislate, efforts continued on Wednesday to try and revive cross-party tax talks which were suspended by the SPD in a recent row over coal subsidies.

The SPD sent a letter to Kohl saying its demand for a two-point cut in unemployment and health insurance charges from this summer must be met before the talks can resume. Waigel said on Tuesday he would respond quickly to the letter.
